Sandra Hüller on that big ‘Digger’ twist, the NYFF double bill of ‘Rose’ and ‘Fatherland,’ and being the ‘Project Hail Mary’ villain Ethan Alter Share on Facebook Post Pin it Show more sharing options Post to Tumblr Submit to Reddit Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Email Print This Page 0 Sandra Hüller knows that moviegoers have seen a lot of her this year. The German actress puts in significant screen time in four 2026 releases, all of which have Oscar ambitions as awards season kicks into gear . While viewers and voters are seeing all of these films within the calendar year, though, taken together they account for two years of Hüller's life. "They've all been made over the course of two years, so it wasn't really the plan to bring them all out in the same year," the actress tells Gold Derby. "The editing process has been very different for each project, and that's why we're all together now. The good thing is that they're very different from each other, so you can't really mix them up!" Sandra Hüller’s Best Actress odds bloom as ‘Rose’ overtakes ‘Fatherland’ at the Oscars and Golden Globes It's certainly true that no single entry in the Hüller Quartet, as it were, is like the other. Her big year began in February when the period drama Rose debuted at the Berlin Film Festival and awarded her the Silver Bear for Best Leading Performance. (Funnily enough, Rose will be the last film to arrive in theaters, opening in general release on Dec. 11.) In March, Hüller was part of Ryan Gosling 's blockbuster space odyssey Project Hail Mary , before traveling back to Cold War-era East Germany in the Cannes-premiering Fatherland , which bows in theaters on Oct. 23 after playing the 2026 New York Film Festival alongside Rose . And she's also among the company that Alejandro G. Iñárritu and Tom Cruise assembled for the divisive Digger , which opened theatrically on Friday. Clearly, Hüller is booked and busy, but she still made time to discuss each of her projects with us — as well as the thread that links these very different works together. Read on for a film-by-film breakdown of the Hüller Quartet. Digger Now that the Digger is out in the world, the truth about its top secret twist can finally be told. Yes, Cruise does play an energy tycoon named Digger Rockwell, whose hubris brings about an apocalyptic climate disaster. But the actor also plays thespian Curtis Markson , who is acting out the part of Digger in a production of a play called Fossil Fools that's being mounted in the dystopian tomorrow that Rockwell brought about. The play-within-a-film conceit is revealed early on in Digger 's runtime with Iñárritu subsequently juxtaposing scenes from Fossil Fools with what's happening to the cast and creative team backstage. For her part, Hüller — who plays the actress playing Digger's half sister, Emma, in Fossil Fools — says that theatrical conceit never really struck her as a plot twist. "The movie has a lot of moments were it surprises people, and things happen that you don't see coming," she allows. "It's playing with our expectations, and I appreciate that. "I think it's a good idea to let it be set where it is set, because it gives other possibilities of storytelling layers and dimensions," the actress adds. "[Theater] is a place that I love to be in, and something that I know about. So I was very happy that Alejandro made that choice." Interestingly, while we learn bits and pieces about Curtis's life when he's not embodying Digger, we only catch a quick glimpse of Hüller's non-Emma persona; following the Fossil Fools curtain call, her unnamed actress celebrates their opening night performance with the rest of the ensemble. "My character doesn't have a second identity," she confirms, adding that she never worked out a backstory for the alter-alter ego. "In that last scene, I had the feeling that Emma would've celebrated the same way, so I didn't make a distinction between them [in my performance]." While the critical response to Digger has been, to put it diplomatically, mixed , Hüller credits Cruise with making the set a welcoming environment. "His enthusiasm was just contagious," she says. "We found the tone of the film together on set as a troop, and that was lovely." Rose The upcoming release of Rose rockets Hüller from the distant future to the distant past; Markus Schleinzer's new film unfolds after the Thirty Years' War roiled 17th century Europe and finds the titular soldier attempting to start a new life with a new identity — as a man. But the actress notes that Rose's concept of her own gender identity is more nuanced than that. "She says in the film that that it's not her goal to be a man," Hüller observes. "I think she's a woman, and that she identifies as a woman. She's putting on a disguise in order to survive in a society that's really dangerous for woman to live in, especially during times of war. It felt like the only choice she had." Despite her best efforts, Rose's ruse doesn't last for long and — given the time period — it shouldn't come as a surprise that the consequences are severe. Still, the film notably refrains from dwelling on the pain and suffering she experiences, preferring to frame her as the hero(ine) of her own story to the bitter end. "The things that happen to her are very cruel," Hüller acknowledges. "But I think of her as someone who is able to protect something inside of her so she's not affected by those things — to the point where she sees them coming, but does what she does anyway, because she knows it's the right thing. That makes her very vulnerable, but also strong at the same time. "And for me personally, I just didn't want to let them win," the actress adds about Rose's tormentors. "So I tried to keep that space inside of me." The final scenes of Rose consciously evoke Carl Theodor Dryer's masterful 1928 silent film, The Passion of Joan of Arc , complete with Rose donning a similar straw crown to the one that actress Renée Jeanne Falconetti's Joan is seen wearing just prior to her execution. But Hüller says that a Passion viewing wasn't part of her pre-shoot preparation. "I didn't know about that film and I still don't know it," she admits. "I have seen a picture of that scene with the crown, because it was very important to Markus. But that's all I know about it." Fatherland Hüller trades the 17th century for the mid-20th century in Paweł Pawlikowski's Fatherland , which follows famed German author Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his adult daughter Erika as they travel from West to East Germany in the years just after World War II, when the memory of the country's Nazi era still looms large. "The strange thing is we didn't talk so much about them as family," the actress says of how the actors and Pawlikowski approached the conceit of placing a father-daughter narrative against the backdrop of a fractured nation. "Maybe we assumed that we all rely on the feelings that we're familiar with in our own families." She and Zischler did rely on letters that the Manns wrote each other during that period to shape that relationship, though. "They wouldn't spare each other from critique, and tell each other the truth at all times," Hüller says of the tone of those written exchanges. "They could be really rude in some moment,s bu they would always forgive each other and move on. That was a really beautiful quality they shared, and we tried to put into our relationship [in the film]." Pawlikowski shared the Best Director prize at Cannes with La Bola Negra helmers Los Javis for his immersive depiction of post-WWII Germany, and Hüller remembers feeling transported back in time during the filming as well. "We shot almost everything in Poland, and it was interesting to be in this place that was obviously affected by the war," she says now. "You can still see the traces of it today, which is very moving and reminds us of the things that happened — and that's a good thing." Project Hail Mary Don't let her karaoke skills fool you — Hüller's Eva Stratt isn't afraid to be the bad guy if it means saving Earth. Midway through Project Hail Mary , we learn that Ryan Gosling's science teacher Ryland Grace didn't exactly volunteer to spearhead a one-way mission to deep space to find a cure for our dying sun. Instead, task force leader Stratt drugged him and blasted his rocket into the final frontier, ensuring that he couldn't say no. "It was pitched to me that way," the actress says of how directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller discussed her character's heel turn. "I got the question early on if I would be fine with her making that decision, and I felt that she literally had no other choice. But what I wanted for her was to not be looked at differently in hindsight. That's not a plan that she had all the time; it's something she needed to decide very fast in order to save humanity. So I wanted her to be aware of the gravity of the choice, and the impact it had on Ryan's character." Because all of Eva's scenes with Ryland happen on Earth, Hüller never got to see the spaceship-set material — including all of Grace's scenes with his alien buddy, Rocky — until she watched the finished movie. "They told me a little bit about it, and I had seen some of the sets, but the scale of it was not something I expected," she says. "Also, the idea of how intense it must have been for Ryan to basically be alone all that time for months. For the whole team, that was a very different period of the filming process and they were so happy when they could leave the studio!" So having been part of two films set in the future and two films set in the past, what has Hüller learned about the present? "All in all, I learned even more about how to honor the past and learn from it," the actress says with a smile about living in 2026. "And how to shape the future and really consciously decide what we want to keep and what can go. Also, to treat each other with respect — and the planet as well." https://www.politico.eu/article/starlink.text: SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services have been restored in Ukraine, allowing the country's forces to operate drones at high speed, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday. "The Ministry of Defense's monitoring systems indicate that Starlink/Starshield speeds have been restored," Khmara told reporters in WhatsApp messages. "We are recording speeds exceeding 400 km/h, and the connection is stable." Since last week, Kyiv had been reporting speed limits on Starshield, Starlink's military-grade service, affecting Ukraine's ability to use drones and carry out defensive strikes. The throttling came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump blaming President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the continuation of the war with Russia. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham raised the issue in a phone call with Trump on Friday. "This outcome is of primary importance for the front line, our military personnel, the operation of drones, logistics, and communications," Khmara said. He added that the ministry of defense would continue to "monitor and track the performance of Starlink/Starshield."
